title: Bandung, April 1955
subtitle: The Asian-African Conference at Gedung Merdeka, Bandung, Indonesia, 18–24 April 1955
intro: In April 1955 the delegations of twenty-nine Asian and African governments met in a converted colonial club in Bandung, West Java, renamed Gedung Merdeka, the Freedom Building, for the week. Five prime ministers had called them there: Nehru of India, Kotelawala of Ceylon, U Nu of Burma, Mohammad Ali of Pakistan and Ali Sastroamidjojo of Indonesia, who had met at Bogor at the end of December 1954. They invited the People's Republic of China, Japan, Egypt and the new or nearly new states of the Middle East, South and Southeast Asia and Africa; they did not invite Israel, South Africa, Taiwan or either Korea. Roughly half the delegations came from governments allied to the United States, a few from communist states, and the rest from governments trying to stay outside both blocs.

No European or American government sat in the room, and that was the point. Washington watched by telegram, briefing its friends while saying in public that the meeting was none of its concern. The People's Republic came under a shadow: on 11 April the Kashmir Princess, an Air India charter carrying members of the Chinese delegation and journalists, was destroyed by a bomb over the South China Sea. Zhou Enlai was not aboard. Beijing blamed American and Nationalist Chinese agents; Taipei denied it; the Hong Kong police later named a suspect who had fled to Taiwan. This chapter reports those positions and the inquiries without deciding between them.

The private record of the room is thin. The Political Committee, where the real arguments happened, met in closed session, and no delegate's diary of the week has been published. What survives are speeches printed by the host government, the Chinese delegation's hour-by-hour cables to Beijing, Nehru's dated letters and notes to India's chief ministers, the American ambassador's telegrams and the Secretary of State's briefings, and the work of the people outside the door: the African American correspondent Ethel Payne, the novelist Richard Wright, Congressman Adam Clayton Powell Jr., and the China specialist A. Doak Barnett, who reconstructed the closed sessions from lobby briefings. Several of the most quoted accounts, by Kotelawala, Romulo and Wright, were written a year later, and they are marked as such.

The week's arguments were about words. Was Soviet rule in Eastern Europe colonialism, as Kotelawala insisted on 21 April? Should new states join military pacts, as Turkey, Pakistan and the Philippines had, or keep out, as Nehru argued? Could communist China be trusted by its neighbours? The answers came as phrases: Zhou's offer to seek common ground, colonialism 'in all its manifestations', and ten principles that put racial equality and non-interference beside the right of collective self-defence. Every eye here read those phrases differently, and the differences are the chapter.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. Bandung and Jakarta kept Indonesian time, roughly twelve hours ahead of Washington, so a telegram sent from Jakarta at 10 p.m. on 23 April reached a Washington still in the morning of the same day; Washington's reactions dated 23 April were written after the Bandung events of that day. Several of the most cited accounts (Kotelawala 1956, Romulo 1956, Wright 1956, Payne 1987) were written well after the week and are placed on the day they describe, with confidence marked 'approx' where the day is inferred.

eyes.name: Sukarno
eyes.role: President of the Republic of Indonesia, aged 53; host of the conference
eyes.authenticity: The opening address of 18 April 1955 was printed by the Indonesian Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Asia-Africa Speak from Bandung (Djakarta, 1955), pp. 19–29, and is reproduced by CVCE; the Indonesian National Archives hold speech scripts and film of the day. A public statement, not a private record.
eyes.bio: The nationalist leader who had declared Indonesian independence in 1945 opened the conference with a speech built for the world press: Asia and Africa as the majority of humanity, colonialism still alive in new forms, and the hope that the new states could press for peace. His country had won recognition from the Dutch only five years earlier, and the communiqué would back its claim to West Irian.

sources.title: Opening address given by Sukarno (Bandung, 18 April 1955), CVCE
Speech at the Opening of the Bandung Conference (excerpts), Internet Modern History Sourcebook

eyes.name: Jawaharlal Nehru
eyes.role: Prime Minister and Minister of External Affairs of India, aged 65; one of the five sponsoring prime ministers
eyes.vantage_label: sponsor and chief architect of non-alignment
eyes.form: dated letters to chief ministers; dated official note; parliamentary statements
eyes.authenticity: Nehru's fortnightly letters to the chief ministers of the Indian states are edited in Letters to Chief Ministers 1947–1964, vol. 4 (1954–1957); the run includes letters of 14 April and 20 May 1955 and a special note on the conference dated 28 April 1955. His statements to the Lok Sabha of 30 April and 2 August 1955 are in the parliamentary debates. These were written for officials and Parliament, so they are careful and partisan to India's line.
eyes.bio: Nehru wanted the meeting to show that the new states could stand outside both Cold War blocs, and to bring the People's Republic of China into the company of Asian governments. His letters show a man who saw himself as the conference's manager, and who privately rated the delegations by how hard they pushed against him.

sources.title: Letters to Chief Ministers 1947–1964, vol. 4 (Digital Library of India text)
Lok Sabha debates, 30 April 1955 (statement on the Asian-African Conference)
Lok Sabha debates, 2 August 1955 (statement on the Kashmir Princess)

eyes.name: Zhou Enlai
eyes.role: Premier and Foreign Minister of the People's Republic of China, aged 57; head of the Chinese delegation
eyes.form: speeches and public statements (official texts); foreign-ministry records
eyes.authenticity: The supplementary speech of 19 April is held in the PRC Foreign Ministry Archives (file 207-00006-02) and was printed in China and the Asian-African Conference (Documents) (Peking: Foreign Languages Press, 1955); the Wilson Center Digital Archive carries an English translation. Records released from the PRC Foreign Ministry Archives are a selection made by that ministry.
eyes.bio: Zhou came to his first great conference outside the communist world a week after a charter plane carrying members of his delegation was destroyed in the air. He chose a soft register: he declined to argue ideology, offered talks on dual nationality and, on the last full day, offered to negotiate with the United States over the Taiwan area.

sources.title: Supplementary speech of Premier Zhou Enlai at the plenary session (19 April 1955), Wilson Center Digital Archive
Minutes of conversation, John Addis and Zhang Yue (16 April 1955), Wilson Center Digital Archive

eyes.name: Zhang Hanfu
eyes.role: Vice Minister of Foreign Affairs of the PRC; member of the Chinese delegation who sent the daily cables home
eyes.where: The Chinese delegation's villa and the conference halls, Bandung
eyes.authenticity: Priority cables from Bandung to Beijing, forwarded to Liu Shaoqi and the Party and ministry departments; held in the PRC Foreign Ministry Archives and published in English translation by the Wilson Center Digital Archive. They are hour-by-hour logs of meetings rather than reflective writing, and they record only what the delegation chose to report.
eyes.bio: Zhang's cables are the nearest thing the room has to a diary: clock times for every breakfast call, lunch, committee and nightcap of the Chinese delegation. They show how much of Bandung happened outside the hall, in villas and at dinners.

sources.title: Cable from Zhang Hanfu, first daily report (19 April 1955)
Cable from Zhang Hanfu, daily report (21 April 1955)
Cable from Zhang Hanfu, daily activities log (23 April 1955)

eyes.name: Sir John Kotelawala
eyes.role: Prime Minister of Ceylon, aged 57; one of the five sponsoring prime ministers
eyes.authenticity: His Political Committee speech was delivered in closed session and is known from delegates' and diplomats' reports (the State Department editors date it 21 April) and from his own memoir, An Asian Prime Minister's Story (London, 1956), which is a self-justifying account written a year later. The well-known exchange with Nehru after the session survives only in later retellings.
eyes.bio: A planter-politician who led Ceylon's conservative United National Party, Kotelawala had co-sponsored the conference with Nehru, then used it to demand that Soviet control of Eastern Europe be condemned alongside Western colonial rule. His intervention set the terms of the week's hardest argument.

sources.title: Memorandum of conversation, Malik and the Secretary of State, 5 May 1955 (FRUS 1955–57 XXI, doc. 51, n. 3 dates the speech)
'When Sir John Kotelawala crossed Nehru', Sunday Observer (Colombo)

eyes.name: Carlos P. Romulo
eyes.role: Head of the Philippine delegation, aged 57; President Magsaysay's special envoy; former President of the UN General Assembly
eyes.side: Philippines; aligned with the United States (Manila Pact/SEATO)
eyes.form: speeches; reports to the US embassy (recorded by others); book (written later)
eyes.authenticity: His speeches are printed in the conference collections; his own account is The Meaning of Bandung (Chapel Hill: University of North Carolina Press, 1956), from lectures given after the conference, which also prints the Final Communiqué. What he told the American ambassador on 23 April survives in Ambassador Cumming's telegram (FRUS). A later memoir (1986) adds recollections.
eyes.bio: Journalist, soldier on MacArthur's staff and veteran UN diplomat, Romulo was the most eloquent defender of alliance with the West in the hall. He attacked colonialism and racism and, in the same breath, communism as a new empire, and he argued with Nehru in open committee.

sources.title: The Meaning of Bandung (1956), University of the Philippines library record
Telegram from the Ambassador in Indonesia (Cumming), 23 April 1955, FRUS 1955–57 II, doc. 216
L. E. Claudio, 'The Anti-Communist Third World: Carlos Romulo and the other Bandung', Southeast Asian Studies 4:1 (2015)

eyes.name: Gamal Abdel Nasser
eyes.role: Prime Minister of Egypt, aged 37, on his first major journey abroad
eyes.authenticity: His conference speech is printed in the conference collections and summarised in the British embassy's telegram of 26 April 1955 (UK National Archives, via CVCE). No private diary of Bandung by Nasser is known; his meetings appear in other delegations' records.
eyes.bio: The young officer who had taken power in Cairo flew to Indonesia with Nehru and came home a figure on the world stage. At Bandung he pressed for Palestine and North African independence and helped broker the compromise wording on colonialism.

sources.title: Summary of the introductory speeches at the Bandung Conference (British Embassy, Djakarta, 26 April 1955), CVCE
Engelsberg Ideas, 'Bandung and the birth of non-alignment'

eyes.name: Takasaki Tatsunosuke
eyes.role: Japanese Minister of State and head of the Economic Planning Agency, aged 70; head of the Japanese delegation
eyes.side: Japan; aligned with the United States
eyes.form: speech (reported); meeting recorded by the Chinese delegation
eyes.authenticity: His opening speech is summarised in the British embassy telegram and in A. Doak Barnett's report; his early-morning call on Zhou Enlai on 22 April appears in Zhang Hanfu's log. No published diary of his has been used here.
eyes.bio: An industrialist turned cabinet minister, Takasaki led the first large Japanese delegation to an Asian gathering since 1945. His speech was modest, expressed regret for wartime damage and stressed trade, and he used the week to open a quiet channel to the PRC.

sources.title: Summary of the introductory speeches (British Embassy, Djakarta), CVCE
Cable from Zhang Hanfu, daily activities log (23 April 1955)

eyes.name: Charles Habib Malik
eyes.role: Lebanese philosopher-diplomat, ambassador to the United States and the UN; member of Lebanon's delegation under Prime Minister Sami Solh
eyes.form: record of conversation (kept by the State Department); lectures
eyes.authenticity: His views after Bandung survive in the State Department memorandum of his conversation with the Secretary of State on 5 May 1955 (FRUS), drafted by an American official, so the wording is the drafter's. His own reflections appeared in The Problem of Coexistence (Mars Lectures, Northwestern University, 1955).
eyes.bio: A co-drafter of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Malik worked in Bandung with Romulo, Turkey's Zorlu and Thailand's Prince Wan in the Western-aligned group. Back in Washington he told Dulles that the real winner had been Communist China.

sources.title: Memorandum of a conversation, 5 May 1955, FRUS 1955–57 XXI, doc. 51

eyes.name: Richard Wright
eyes.role: American novelist (Native Son, Black Boy), aged 46, living in Paris; attended as a freelance journalist
eyes.side: African American writer in exile; unaligned observer
eyes.authenticity: The Color Curtain: A Report on the Bandung Conference (1956) was written after the trip; Indonesian writers who met him later contested parts of his account. His lecture 'The Artist and His Problems', given in Jakarta before he left, survived only in Indonesian until it was recovered in Indonesian Notebook (Duke, 2016). The trip was financed with help from the Congress for Cultural Freedom.
eyes.bio: Wright read about the conference in a Paris newspaper in December 1954 and decided at once to go. He saw Bandung as a meeting of the world's colonised and coloured peoples defined by race and religion as much as by politics, and his book is the outsider's classic account of the week.

sources.title: B. R. Roberts and K. Foulcher, 'Richard Wright and the Bandung Conference', ASAA
Indonesian Notebook: A Sourcebook on Richard Wright and the Bandung Conference (Duke, 2016)

eyes.name: Adam Clayton Powell Jr.
eyes.role: US Congressman for Harlem and pastor of Abyssinian Baptist Church, aged 46; attended on press credentials as an unofficial observer
eyes.form: press statements and newspaper reports; memoir (written later)
eyes.authenticity: Known from contemporary African American newspaper reports (e.g. Memphis World, 26 April 1955), Ethel Payne's recollections, State Department records that mention his trip, and his memoir Adam by Adam (1971). Accounts by his son (2026) add family recollection but cite no documents.
eyes.bio: The State Department did not want him to go; he went anyway, sponsored by the Black press, and in Bandung defended the United States as a country changing its racial order while attacking Jim Crow at home. He chased a meeting with Zhou Enlai through the week.

sources.title: Memphis World, 26 April 1955 (Rhodes College digital collection)
Telephone call, Dulles to Wisner, 1 April 1955, FRUS 1955–57 XXI, doc. 40
A. C. Powell III, 'Seen and Unseen' (2026)

eyes.name: Ethel L. Payne
eyes.role: Washington correspondent of the Chicago Defender, aged 43
eyes.vantage_label: reporter with 'a box seat on history'
eyes.authenticity: Her dispatches ran in the Chicago Defender in April–May 1955; her recollections were recorded by Kathleen Currie for the Washington Press Club Foundation's Women in Journalism oral history project on 22 September 1987, more than thirty years later, and are marked by that distance.
eyes.bio: Sent by publisher John Sengstacke to what he called the first conference of the world's darker peoples, Payne filed through couriers to Jakarta. Her memories are of the human texture: Powell's jokes, Wright improvising with her hot comb, students greeting her as 'the American Negro'.

sources.title: Ethel Payne oral history, interview 4, Washington Press Club Foundation

eyes.name: A. Doak Barnett
eyes.role: American China specialist, aged 33, reporting for the American Universities Field Staff
eyes.authenticity: 'Random Notes on the Asian-African Conference', written at the Hotel Simpang, Surabaya, on 18 May 1955 and circulated by the American Universities Field Staff; the scan is held by the Institute of Current World Affairs. Closed sessions are reconstructed from delegations' briefings, as he says.
eyes.bio: Born in China to missionary parents, Barnett could not get an interview with Zhou, but he watched him at public events and at Nehru's house, and he logged the closed sessions day by day from what delegations told the press.

sources.title: A. Doak Barnett, 'Random Notes on the Asian-African Conference' (ADB-78), ICWA

eyes.name: John Foster Dulles
eyes.role: US Secretary of State, aged 67, and the department he directed
eyes.authenticity: Printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, 1952–54 vol. XII and 1955–57 vols. II, XXI and XXII, from State Department central files and the Eisenhower Library. US-government records, quoted here within twelve words. Some items were signed by Under Secretary Hoover or drafted by subordinates in Dulles's name.
eyes.bio: Dulles publicly called the meeting no direct concern of the United States while the department prepared friendly delegations, asked the CIA what it was doing, and briefed the Cabinet afterwards. The American record is the fullest outside view of the conference, and it is a record of worry.

sources.title: FRUS 1955–57 vol. XXI, chapter 1: The Afro-Asian (Bandung) Conference
Minutes of a Cabinet meeting, 29 April 1955, FRUS 1955–57 XXI, doc. 48

entries.headline: Five prime ministers at Bogor agree to call the conference
entries.digest: Nehru, Kotelawala, U Nu, Mohammad Ali of Pakistan and Ali Sastroamidjojo met for two days at Bogor and agreed to hold an Asian-African conference in Indonesia in April 1955. Their communiqué of 29 December named twenty-five further countries to be invited, so that thirty governments in all were asked; the Central African Federation declined, leaving twenty-nine. Nehru later told Parliament that Indonesia had carried most of the organisation.
entries.source_note: Dates from the ANRI Memory of the World nomination (Five-Country Conference, 28–29 Dec 1954); communiqué date and 25 invitees from FRUS 1952–54 XII doc. 433 n. 2–3; Nehru, Lok Sabha 30 Apr 1955. The Central African Federation's refusal is widely reported but was not seen in a primary source here.

entries.headline: Washington says the conference is not its business, privately worries
entries.digest: Dulles told his press conference that the planned meeting did not directly concern the United States, which was neither Asian nor African nor invited. The same day a secret circular told American posts that the department was seriously concerned that Beijing would use the meeting to show a false unity between communist and non-communist Asia, and instructed them to stay noncommittal in public and not push friends to refuse.
entries.source_note: FRUS 1952–54 XII part 1, doc. 433 (telegram 340, 31 Dec 1954, 4:10 p.m.).

entries.headline: Briefing friendly delegations without seeming to run them
entries.digest: A circular telegram, sent over Under Secretary Hoover's name, set out how friendly governments might handle the conference: expect Chinese lobbying and anti-colonial propaganda, answer with Korea, Vietnam and forced labour in communist states, stress American aid, but avoid any look of American control and never start a quarrel. Consultations were to be oral, with no papers handed over.
entries.source_note: FRUS 1955–57 XXI, doc. 23 (circular telegram 491, 25 Feb 1955, 8:36 p.m.).

entries.headline: Dulles asks the CIA what it is doing about Bandung
entries.digest: In a telephone call Dulles asked Frank Wisner of the CIA whether enough imaginative thought was going into the conference. Wisner said an interdepartmental committee was at work and the agency had people in the field; both men agreed that Congressman Adam Clayton Powell's planned trip was not helpful. A promised note on CIA activities was never found in State Department files.
entries.quote: They have irons in the fire in the field
entries.source_note: FRUS 1955–57 XXI, doc. 40 (memorandum of telephone conversation, 1 Apr 1955, 12:57 p.m.).

entries.place: South China Sea, off the Natuna Islands
entries.headline: The Kashmir Princess is destroyed in the air
entries.digest: The Air India Constellation chartered to carry members of the Chinese delegation and journalists from Hong Kong to Jakarta caught fire after an explosion and came down in the sea; sixteen people died and three crew members survived. Zhou was not aboard: his own journey ran through Rangoon. The PRC government declared the crash a murder by the special services of the United States and Chiang Kai-shek. The Republic of China denied any part in it; Hong Kong police later named an airport cleaner who had fled to Taiwan, which refused extradition. American officials denied involvement, and historians still debate who knew what and whether Zhou had been warned.
entries.source_note: Kashmir Princess article (IPFS mirror of Wikipedia), citing the Indonesian inquiry, Hong Kong police findings, PRC statements and S. Tsang's research; Nehru, Lok Sabha 2 Aug 1955. The date of the first PRC statement (generally given as 12 April) was not checked against the text.

entries.headline: Wright lands in Indonesia
entries.digest: Richard Wright arrived for a stay of more than three weeks. He had read about the conference in a Paris newspaper the previous December and arranged the trip at once, partly paid for by the Congress for Cultural Freedom. Indonesian writers and editors took him in hand, and the press tracked his movements around Jakarta before the delegations arrived.
entries.source_note: Roberts and Foulcher, ASAA article (12 April–5 May 1955).

entries.headline: Nehru writes to the chief ministers on the eve of departure
entries.digest: Leaving that night with Egypt's prime minister and Afghanistan's foreign minister, to pick up U Nu in Rangoon, Nehru told the chief ministers that the loss of the Air India Constellation three days earlier was a great blow, and declined to say more while it was under inquiry. He expected the conference to stick to general principles and peace, warned that disputes between members could not be settled by votes, and described Formosa and the offshore islands as still dangerous.
entries.source_note: Letters to Chief Ministers, vol. 4, letter 22 (14 Apr 1955).

entries.headline: A congressman holds court at Manila airport
entries.digest: On the way out Payne first saw Adam Clayton Powell giving a press conference about the conference at Manila airport, and flew on with him and Carlos Romulo. Arriving in Indonesia, she was greeted by students as 'the American Negro'; Powell joked that he was coloured too.
entries.source_note: Ethel Payne oral history, interview 4 (22 Sept 1987). The exact day of the Manila stop is not given.

entries.headline: Weather forces Zhou's plane down at Singapore
entries.digest: Zhou's aircraft bound for Indonesia landed at Singapore because of weather and had not left by mid-afternoon. In Beijing a Foreign Ministry official asked the British chargé d'affaires to have the Singapore authorities guard the premier and the plane and keep people away from it; the British diplomat promised to pass the request on at once. Five days after the Kashmir Princess, the request needed no explanation.
entries.source_note: Minutes of conversation, John Addis and Zhang Yue, 16 Apr 1955, 4:45 p.m. (PRC Foreign Ministry Archives via Wilson Center).

entries.headline: The Chinese arrive, and Nehru and U Nu call at once
entries.digest: Zhang's first cable recorded the delegation's arrival in Bandung on the 17th and a visit to the villa by Nehru and U Nu, followed by Indonesia's foreign minister. A separate Chinese record of a talk with Nehru and U Nu (archived under 16 April) has the three discussing procedure: Nehru doubted that twenty-nine divided countries could run a permanent body, U Nu wanted only general principles, and Zhou proposed a loose liaison office in Jakarta.
entries.source_note: Cable from Zhang Hanfu, first daily report (19 Apr 1955, covering 17–18 Apr); summary of talks between Zhou, Nehru and U Nu (Wilson Center; dated 16 Apr in the archive, which conflicts with the Singapore diversion that day).

entries.headline: Sukarno opens the first intercontinental conference of coloured peoples
entries.digest: Sukarno told the delegates that this was the first intercontinental meeting of coloured peoples in history. He recalled that on another 18 April, in 1775, Paul Revere had ridden out at the start of an anti-colonial war, warned that colonialism had a modern dress of economic and intellectual control, and argued that Asia and Africa, the majority of mankind, could press the nuclear powers for peace. He closed with 'live and let live' and the call for unity in diversity.
entries.quote: I say to you, colonialism is not yet dead.
entries.source_note: Opening address, Asia-Africa Speak from Bandung (Djakarta, 1955), pp. 19–29, via CVCE.

entries.headline: Sukarno quotes Washington and Lincoln to the press seats
entries.digest: Payne remembered Sukarno as a great orator who reached for George Washington and Abraham Lincoln in his opening. Indonesian soldiers on guard raised their bayonets to let her pass each morning and lowered them for Chet Huntley of NBC, who argued with them. Her first story went to Jakarta by courier under the headline 'Freedom Fever Sweeps Bandung'.
entries.source_note: Ethel Payne oral history, interview 4 (1987). The date of the first dispatch is not given.

entries.headline: Wright watches the world's underdogs take their seats
entries.digest: In The Color Curtain Wright treated the opening as a meeting defined by race and religion more than by Cold War politics: delegates who had been colonial subjects now spoke as governments, in a city decorated with flags and crowded with onlookers. He quoted Sukarno at length and read the speech as an appeal to shared racial memory.
entries.source_note: Wright, The Color Curtain (1956), Bandung chapters; not a dated diary, so the day is that of the speech he describes.

entries.headline: Opening day logged: every delegation but three has called
entries.digest: Zhang reported that the conference opened with a meeting of delegation heads and that Sukarno gave a reception that evening. By the end of the second day heads of every delegation except (South) Vietnam, Saudi Arabia and Ethiopia had been in contact with Zhou. He added that there had been no security problems in Bandung.
entries.source_note: Cable from Zhang Hanfu, first daily report (19 Apr 1955).

entries.headline: Nasser speaks for Palestine and North Africa
entries.digest: In his opening statement Nasser called for cooperation against colonialism, support for the UN Charter, disarmament and an end to racial discrimination in South Africa, and put the case of the Palestinian Arabs and of Morocco, Tunisia and Algeria before the conference. The British embassy's summary placed him among the most forceful speakers on the Arab questions.
entries.source_note: British Embassy Djakarta telegram, 26 Apr 1955 (summary of introductory speeches, 18–19 Apr), via CVCE. The summary does not say which of the two days each delegate spoke.

entries.headline: Ceylon's opening: the conference on the brink
entries.digest: Kotelawala's opening statement warned that the meeting stood at the edge of failure and argued that Asian and African nations could act as mediators between the communist and anti-communist worlds. He asked for wider UN membership and for development help. The speech gave no hint of the attack on Soviet policy he would make two days later.
entries.source_note: British Embassy Djakarta telegram, 26 Apr 1955, via CVCE.

entries.headline: Japan apologises and talks trade
entries.digest: Takasaki apologised for the absence of Prime Minister Hatoyama and gave a modest, uncontroversial speech. Barnett recorded that it expressed regret for the damage Japan had done in the war; it stressed democracy, peace, economic development and cultural exchange. Japan voted with the Western-aligned group through the week.
entries.source_note: British Embassy Djakarta telegram, 26 Apr 1955; Barnett, 'Random Notes' (18 May 1955).

entries.headline: Romulo: a police state can be as bad as a colony
entries.digest: Romulo urged realism over propaganda, condemned racial discrimination, especially in South Africa, and warned that a police state could be as oppressive as colonial rule. He set Western colonialism and communist expansion side by side as dangers to new nations. Barnett heard it as one of the conference's most eloquent speeches.
entries.source_note: British Embassy Djakarta telegram, 26 Apr 1955; Philippines Free Press report cited in Claudio (2015); Barnett, 'Random Notes'. Day inferred from the alphabetical order of speakers.

entries.headline: Zhou drops his script and seeks common ground
entries.digest: After two days of speeches in which the Philippines, Pakistan, Turkey, Thailand and Iraq attacked communism, Zhou circulated his prepared speech in writing and spoke briefly instead. He granted that Chinese communists believed in their system but said ideology was not the business of the meeting; shared suffering under colonialism was. He promised respect for religious belief, denied that China subverted its neighbours, offered to settle the dual nationality of overseas Chinese, and invited delegates to come and see China for themselves.
entries.quote: to seek common ground, not to create divergence
entries.source_note: Supplementary speech, 19 Apr 1955 (PRC FMA 207-00006-02; China and the Asian-African Conference, Peking 1955, pp. 21–27), via Wilson Center; time of day from Barnett.

entries.headline: The plenary turns, and Zhou speaks last
entries.digest: Barnett noted that the opening plenaries ran in alphabetical order and that Romulo and Mohammad Ali pressed hard anti-communist lines, followed by Zorlu of Turkey and Prince Wan of Thailand. Zhou held back until the afternoon of the 19th. From then on the meeting moved behind closed doors to the Pension Fund building, where delegations briefed reporters in the lobbies.
entries.source_note: Barnett, 'Random Notes on the Asian-African Conference' (written 18 May 1955).

entries.headline: Wright reads Zhou's moderation as strategy
entries.digest: Wright reproduced much of Zhou's short speech in his book and treated it as a lesson in tactics: the communist premier had spoken the language of race and anti-colonial grievance that united the hall rather than the language of ideology that divided it. He was struck that the most feared delegate had sounded the most conciliatory.
entries.source_note: Wright, The Color Curtain (1956). Paraphrase of the book's treatment; not a dated entry.

entries.headline: Committees form; Palestine goes to a drafting group
entries.digest: At 8 a.m. a students' choir welcomed the delegates. The heads of delegation sat as the Political Committee from 9 to noon and from 3 until after 7, and set up an eight-country drafting committee on Palestine while the economic and cultural committees met. Zhou lunched with Prince Sihanouk; in the evening Nehru gave dinner for Zhou and the heads of the Thai, Philippine and Saudi delegations.
entries.source_note: Cable from Zhang Hanfu, daily report (21 Apr 1955, covering 20–21 Apr).

entries.headline: Defending America abroad, attacking Jim Crow at home
entries.digest: Powell, holding press credentials rather than an official post, spoke to reporters and delegates as a Black American who could describe both segregation and the fight against it. Film from Bandung shows him saying the Soviet Union was as racist as the United States, but that Americans were working to change. An Atlanta Daily World columnist called him the ghost of democracy at the conference.
entries.source_note: A. C. Powell III, 'Seen and Unseen' (2026), describing a film clip; William Gordon, 'The Ghost at Bandung', Atlanta Daily World (reprinted in Memphis World collection). Powell, Adam by Adam (1971).

entries.headline: Kotelawala names Soviet colonialism
entries.digest: In the closed committee on colonialism Kotelawala asked why the Soviet-controlled states of Eastern Europe and Central Asia should not be counted as colonies just as surely as any territory in Africa or Asia, and proposed that the conference oppose Soviet colonialism alongside Western imperialism. In his memoir Kotelawala recalled Nehru asking afterwards why he had not shown him the speech, and answering that Nehru never showed him his.
entries.source_note: Date: FRUS 1955–57 XXI doc. 51 n. 3; content: Barnett; Claudio citing Kotelawala, An Asian Prime Minister's Story (1956), pp. 187–188; the exchange with Nehru as retold in the Sunday Observer (2023).

entries.headline: The East–West quarrel Nehru wanted to avoid
entries.digest: Barnett recorded Kotelawala's Thursday speech on Soviet control of Eastern Europe as the moment the Cold War entered the room. It produced a sharp procedural dispute and the issue was put off, which pleased nobody: Western-aligned delegates wanted a vote, and Nehru wanted the subject gone.
entries.source_note: Barnett, 'Random Notes' (18 May 1955).

entries.headline: Pham Van Dong at breakfast, Mohammad Ali after lunch
entries.digest: Zhang logged an 8:30 a.m. call on Zhou by Pham Van Dong, vice-premier of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam. At 2 p.m. Zhou visited Pakistan's prime minister Mohammad Ali, whose government was in the Manila Pact; at 3 p.m. Vice-Premier Chen Yi sat on the West Irian drafting committee. That evening Nasser gave dinner for Zhou, U Nu and the Nepalese delegation head.
entries.source_note: Cable from Zhang Hanfu, daily report (21 Apr 1955).

entries.headline: Nasser hosts Zhou and U Nu
entries.digest: Nasser invited Zhou, U Nu and Nepal's delegation head to dinner. Nothing of what was said appears in the Chinese log; later accounts trace to Bandung the first contacts that led Egypt toward arms from the Soviet bloc, which came in a deal with Czechoslovakia that September.
entries.source_note: Cable from Zhang Hanfu, daily report (21 Apr 1955); Engelsberg Ideas on the September 1955 Czech arms deal. The content of the dinner talk is not recorded in sources seen.

entries.headline: Nehru defends non-alignment against the pact members
entries.digest: Nehru spoke at length in the Political Committee for keeping out of military blocs, arguing that it degraded newly freed nations to line up as followers of either camp, and clashed with Turkey, Pakistan and the Philippines, whose governments belonged to NATO, the Baghdad Pact or the Manila Pact. He later withdrew some of his sharpest words. In his note of 28 April he counted three speeches of his in the committee.
entries.source_note: Barnett, 'Random Notes' (Friday 22 April, deadlock); Nehru, note of 28 Apr 1955 in Letters to Chief Ministers vol. 4. The Political Committee met in closed session; no verbatim record was consulted.

entries.headline: Romulo answers Nehru
entries.digest: Romulo replied that communist expansion was openly declared policy rather than a slander invented by its enemies, that communist parties did not respect elections, and that India too should look to its northern frontier. He set the old empires against a new communist one, and years later recorded that Nehru told him he had been right at Bandung.
entries.source_note: Romulo, The Meaning of Bandung (1956), pp. 31–33, 82–88, and memoir (1986), p. 139, as cited by Claudio (2015). The day is inferred from Barnett's account of Friday's debate.

entries.headline: Friday: deadlock
entries.digest: Barnett called Friday the low point. Nehru's long defence of neutralism drew sharp answers from the Western-aligned delegates; Romulo, Mohammad Ali, Zorlu, Prince Wan and Charles Malik worked as a group, and the committee seemed unable to agree on either colonialism or coexistence. Reporters in the lobbies began writing of failure.
entries.source_note: Barnett, 'Random Notes' (18 May 1955).

entries.headline: Japan at 7:40, a treaty at 8:30, Nehru at 10:25 p.m.
entries.digest: Zhang's log for the 22nd began with a call on Zhou and Chen Yi by Takasaki's party from 7:40 to 8:30, followed by the signing of the Sino-Indonesian treaty on dual nationality. A drafting committee on colonialism was created that day. After dinners and receptions given by Sudan and Saudi Arabia, Zhou went to Nehru's residence at 10:25 p.m. to talk about Indochina with India, Burma and the four Indochinese states.
entries.source_note: Cable from Zhang Hanfu, daily activities log (23 Apr 1955, covering 22 Apr).

entries.headline: A breakfast call that reopens a door
entries.digest: Before the day's sessions Takasaki's party called on Zhou and Chen Yi for fifty minutes. The Chinese log does not say what was discussed, but it was among the first direct contacts between the two governments since the war, and Takasaki would later be one of the Japanese politicians who built informal trade ties with the PRC.
entries.source_note: Cable from Zhang Hanfu, daily activities log (23 Apr 1955). The log names 'representatives from Takasaki'; whether Takasaki attended in person is not stated.

entries.headline: Signing the dual-nationality treaty
entries.digest: Zhou and Indonesia's foreign minister Sunario signed a treaty under which Chinese residents of Indonesia would choose one nationality. It answered one of the fears voiced against China in the plenary, that the overseas Chinese were a fifth column.
entries.source_note: Cable from Zhang Hanfu (23 Apr 1955); Wikipedia mirror on the conference (Sunario as signatory).

entries.place: Luncheon of the Colombo powers, China, the Philippines and Thailand, Bandung
entries.headline: Kotelawala asks Zhou about the Taiwan Strait
entries.digest: At a private luncheon Kotelawala asked Zhou how tension over Taiwan might be eased. As relayed to the American ambassador, Zhou answered that Taiwan was an internal Chinese matter, that China did not want war and would negotiate with the United States, but that the United States and Chiang must in the end leave the island.
entries.source_note: Telegram from Ambassador Cumming, 23 Apr 1955, 10 p.m., FRUS 1955–57 II doc. 216 (Romulo's report of the luncheon).

entries.headline: Zhou offers to talk to the United States
entries.digest: That afternoon the Chinese delegation issued a short public statement: China did not want war with the United States and was willing to sit down with it to discuss relaxing tension in the Far East, especially in the Taiwan area. In committee the same day Zhou proposed a seven-point declaration of peace modelled on the five principles he and Nehru had agreed in 1954.
entries.quote: The Chinese people are friendly to the American people.
entries.source_note: Statement as quoted in FRUS 1955–57 II doc. 216 n. 3 (from the New York Times, 24 Apr 1955); seven points from FRUS 1955–57 XXII doc. 94 n. 10; Barnett.

entries.headline: Romulo calls in the American ambassador
entries.digest: Romulo urgently summoned Ambassador Hugh Cumming to pass on what Zhou had said at the luncheon, declined to comment without instructions from Manila, and asked that the substance go to Washington and to Assistant Secretary Robertson in Taipei. The Chinese public statement arrived while Cumming's telegram was being coded.
entries.quote: Method or forum of negotiation not important
entries.source_note: Telegram from Ambassador Cumming, 23 Apr 1955, 10 p.m., FRUS 1955–57 II doc. 216.

entries.headline: Saturday: the conference swings toward Zhou
entries.digest: Barnett judged Zhou's Saturday speech and his Formosa statement the turning point. A man who had stayed in the background all week became the centre of the conference, with reassurances to his neighbours, a treaty with Indonesia and an offer of talks with Washington; delegates who had come to resist him found themselves praising his reasonableness.
entries.source_note: Barnett, 'Random Notes' (18 May 1955).

entries.headline: A conditional answer from Washington
entries.digest: With the President's press secretary ready to draft a presidential reply, Under Secretary Hoover argued that a presidential comment would give Zhou's offer too much weight; the department instead issued a press release the same day welcoming sincere efforts for peace but setting conditions, including Nationalist China's participation. An internal memo of 25 April judged the offer a move to put the blame for Far Eastern tension on the United States and noted that the conferees were reportedly stunned.
entries.quote: The United States always welcomes any efforts, if sincere
entries.source_note: Sebald to the Secretary, 25 Apr 1955, FRUS 1955–57 II doc. 217.

entries.headline: Sunday: communiqué approved, closing plenary
entries.digest: The heads of delegation approved the final communiqué on Sunday and the conference closed in plenary at the Freedom Building. Barnett noted that the Gold Coast's delegation, led by Kojo Botsio and attending although the colony was not yet sovereign, had voted with the Western-aligned group, as had Japan.
entries.source_note: Barnett, 'Random Notes' (18 May 1955).

entries.headline: Colonialism 'in all its manifestations'
entries.digest: The communiqué's clause on colonialism avoided naming either the Soviet Union or the West, condemning colonialism in all its manifestations as an evil to be ended speedily. Accounts of the drafting credit Nasser with helping find the formula that let both camps sign: the anti-communists could read Eastern Europe into it, Zhou and Nehru could read it as aimed at the old empires.
entries.source_note: Final Communiqué, Section D (reprinted in Romulo 1956, pp. 92–102, per Claudio); Engelsberg Ideas and Nehru's note of 28 Apr (Egypt's prime minister helped reach compromises).

entries.headline: Nehru's closing words
entries.digest: Nehru spoke once at the closing session, after the communiqué and its Declaration on the Promotion of World Peace and Cooperation, read out by Secretary-General Roeslan Abdulgani, had been adopted. He wrote four days later that he would have worded parts differently, but accepted it as a worthy document reached without a single vote.
entries.source_note: Nehru, note on the Asian-African Conference, 28 Apr 1955 (Letters to Chief Ministers vol. 4); ANRI nomination (Abdulgani read the declaration).

entries.headline: Powell gets his handshake with Zhou
entries.digest: After days of trying to arrange a meeting, Powell met Zhou face to face at a party at the Savoy Homann Hotel. Zhou shook his hand; his interpreter said the premier was very tired and very busy. Powell had said that if Zhou had not called by 8 a.m. on Sunday his efforts would be useless, and that he was due to leave for Jakarta that afternoon. Payne remembered him confronting Zhou at a film screening about American airmen held in China.
entries.source_note: Memphis World, 26 Apr 1955 (undated article headed '9 A.M. Sunday'); Payne oral history (1987).

entries.headline: A private scorecard of the delegations
entries.digest: In a special note Nehru counted twenty-nine countries, a huge Japanese delegation, thirty-four Egyptians and some forty Chinese security men, whose presence he tied to the Kashmir Princess. Zhou, he wrote, had been accommodating and lost his temper only once, saying China would not be bullied. Pakistan and Turkey had been the most aggressive delegations, with Iraq and Lebanon close behind; Egypt, Syria and Afghanistan had helped; Thailand and the Philippines had followed the American line and Ceylon leaned that way. He judged the conference a remarkable success.
entries.source_note: Nehru, 'Note on the Asian-African Conference at Bandung', 28 Apr 1955, Letters to Chief Ministers vol. 4, p. 159 ff.

entries.headline: Dulles tells the Cabinet it went better than feared
entries.digest: Dulles reported that the conference had not been dominated by Zhou but by friendly Asian nations, that most of the communiqué was acceptable to the United States except on Palestine, that Nehru had lost prestige while Zhou adapted shrewdly, and that pressure against violence had turned the meeting against a war over Formosa. He noted that the Asian nations had gained a new self-confidence from working together.
entries.quote: dominated by a group of friendly Asian nations
entries.source_note: Minutes of a Cabinet meeting, 29 Apr 1955, FRUS 1955–57 XXI doc. 48.

entries.headline: Reporting to Parliament
entries.digest: Nehru laid the communiqué before the House. He explained that some delegates had wanted independent states counted as colonies, a Cold War argument the final text avoided; that the declaration embodied the Panch Shila, which India accepted in full, while allowing collective self-defence under the UN Charter, which India still opposed in practice; and that Zhou had said he was ready for direct talks with the United States over Formosa.
entries.source_note: Lok Sabha debates, 30 Apr 1955 (eparlib).

entries.headline: A last lecture and departure
entries.digest: Before leaving Indonesia on 5 May Wright gave a lecture in Jakarta on the artist and his problems, which the Indonesian press printed in translation; the English original was lost until 2016. Indonesian writers who had hosted him later wrote their own accounts of the visit, some of them at odds with the version in The Color Curtain, published the following year.
entries.source_note: Roberts and Foulcher, ASAA article; Indonesian Notebook (Duke, 2016), part II. Exact lecture date not seen.

entries.headline: Malik to Dulles: China won friends
entries.digest: Back in Washington, Malik told the Secretary that the main result of Bandung was goodwill for Communist China, which he thought the meeting had been staged to produce, and that American papers were wrong to say Nehru had lost standing. Kotelawala's speech had been a great shock, he said, but Kotelawala then fell silent, as if someone had leaned on him. Malik advised against another such meeting for at least five years; the Secretary partly disagreed, seeing a relaxation of tension.
entries.source_note: Memorandum of a conversation, 5 May 1955 (drafted 10 May), FRUS 1955–57 XXI doc. 51.

entries.headline: Writing it up three weeks later
entries.digest: From Surabaya Barnett wrote his random notes: the motorcades and flags, the troops guarding a city ringed by Darul Islam rebels, several hundred newsmen chasing briefings in villas and lobbies, and a conference that had begun with Nehru's attempts to manage it and ended as Zhou's.
entries.source_note: Barnett, 'Random Notes on the Asian-African Conference' (AUFS, 18 May 1955).

entries.headline: The inquiry reports: a time bomb in the wheel well
entries.digest: Nehru told Parliament that the Indonesian investigation committee had found beyond doubt that a timed explosive device in the starboard wheel well had brought down the Kashmir Princess, and that it could only have been placed during the stop at Hong Kong, where a separate inquiry had made arrests but not concluded. Captain Jatar and stewardess Gloria Berry had been given the Ashoka Chakra posthumously, and the surviving co-pilot was decorated too.
entries.source_note: Lok Sabha debates, 2 Aug 1955 (statement on the crash). The Indonesian board reported on 26 May 1955.

claims.claim: Five Colombo-power prime ministers decide to hold an Asian-African conference in Indonesia in April 1955 and to invite 25 more countries
claims.evidence: Bogor/Djakarta communiqué, cited in FRUS 1952–54 XII doc. 433 nn. 2–3; ANRI nomination

claims.claim: United States declares the conference not its direct concern while privately instructing posts to stay noncommittal
State Department proposes that friendly delegations take constructive, non-provocative positions and rebut communist claims
Conference opened at Gedung Merdeka; Ali Sastroamidjojo elected to preside
claims.evidence: Barnett, 'Random Notes'; Sukarno opening address; ANRI photographs

claims.claim: Zhou proposes that the conference seek common ground and set ideological differences aside
Political Committee sets up an eight-country drafting committee on Palestine
Moves that the conference oppose Soviet colonialism in Eastern Europe alongside Western imperialism
claims.evidence: FRUS 1955–57 XXI doc. 51 n. 3; Barnett; Kotelawala memoir (1956)

claims.claim: The question of Soviet colonialism is deferred after a procedural dispute
Nehru argues against membership of military blocs; Romulo, Zorlu and Mohammad Ali defend collective security
claims.evidence: Barnett; Nehru note of 28 April; Romulo (1956) via Claudio

claims.claim: Sino-Indonesian treaty on dual nationality signed
Offers to negotiate with the United States on easing tension in the Taiwan area; proposes a seven-point peace declaration
claims.evidence: FRUS 1955–57 II doc. 216 n. 3; FRUS 1955–57 XXII doc. 94 n. 10

claims.claim: State Department answers with a conditional press release rather than a presidential statement
Final Communiqué adopted by consensus, without voting; condemns 'colonialism in all its manifestations'
claims.evidence: Nehru note of 28 April; Final Communiqué section D

claims.claim: Declaration on the Promotion of World Peace and Cooperation (ten principles) adopted, including the right of collective self-defence under the UN Charter
claims.evidence: Final Communiqué; Nehru, Lok Sabha 30 April 1955

claims.claim: Communiqué backs Indonesia's position on West Irian and urges the Netherlands to reopen negotiations
Indonesian board of inquiry finds that a time bomb, probably placed at Hong Kong, destroyed the Kashmir Princess
claims.evidence: Nehru, Lok Sabha 2 August 1955; Kashmir Princess article

convergences.label: The Kashmir Princess is lost, a week before the opening
convergences.note: The PRC called the crash a murder by American and Nationalist Chinese special services; Taiwan denied it; Nehru, whose national airline had lost a crew, told his chief ministers it was a great blow but would say no more while it was under inquiry. Four months later he reported the bomb to Parliament without naming who planted it. The forty Chinese security men he counted in Bandung were the crash's shadow over the week.

convergences.label: Opening day at Gedung Merdeka
convergences.note: Sukarno spoke to history and to American memory (Paul Revere, Washington, Lincoln); Payne remembered the oratory and the bayonets; Wright heard a congress of race and religion; Zhang's cable recorded the same day as a list of which delegation heads had called on Zhou. Same speech, four different rooms.

convergences.label: Speeches in alphabetical order; Zhou answers in the afternoon
convergences.note: Romulo set a police state beside a colony, Kotelawala warned of collapse, Takasaki apologised for the war. Zhou's reply refused to argue ideology at all. Barnett and Wright both saw it as the speech of the day, Barnett as diplomacy and Wright as racial solidarity overriding Cold War lines.

convergences.label: Kotelawala raises Soviet colonialism in closed committee
convergences.note: Kotelawala recorded it as plain speaking; Barnett as the moment the Cold War entered the room; Zhang's log for the day is silent on it, listing instead Pham Van Dong's breakfast call and Zhou's visit to Pakistan's prime minister. Two weeks later Malik told Dulles the speech had shocked the hall and that its author then went quiet.

convergences.label: Friday's deadlock: alignment against non-alignment
convergences.note: Nehru and Romulo each remembered winning the argument; Barnett saw a deadlock. Zhang's log shows the other conference running at the same time: Japan's early call on Zhou, the dual-nationality treaty, and Zhou at Nehru's house at 10:25 p.m.

convergences.label: Zhou's offer of talks with the United States
convergences.note: The same offer passed through four filters in one day: Kotelawala's question at lunch, Romulo's urgent call to the American ambassador, Barnett's sense of the room turning, and a Washington press release that welcomed peace if sincere and set conditions.

convergences.label: The communiqué and the ten principles
convergences.note: Adopted without a vote. Nehru would have worded it differently but called it worthy; the formula on colonialism let each camp read its own enemy into it; Barnett counted the Gold Coast and Japan with the Western-aligned side.

convergences.label: The verdicts abroad
convergences.note: Within three weeks the same conference was a success for friendly Asian nations (Dulles to the Cabinet), a remarkable success for Asian-African purpose (Nehru), a gain for Communist China (Malik) and a week in which Zhou took the room from Nehru (Barnett).

ties.note: Nehru called on Zhou the day the Chinese arrived and Zhou came to Nehru's residence late on 22 April to discuss Indochina; Nehru's note praised him as accommodating.
Fellow sponsors since Colombo and Bogor; Kotelawala's speech on Soviet colonialism blindsided Nehru, and the sharp exchange after the session became part of both men's legends.
The two argued over military pacts and neutralism in the Political Committee; Romulo later wrote that Nehru conceded the point years afterwards.
Romulo drew on Kotelawala's charge about Eastern Europe in his own case against communist 'empire', and both sat at the 23 April luncheon with Zhou.
At the luncheon of 23 April Kotelawala asked Zhou how to ease the Taiwan Strait crisis; the answer reached Washington the same night.
Nasser flew out of Delhi with Nehru on 14 April; Nehru's note credited Egypt's prime minister with brokering compromises.
Takasaki's party called on Zhou and Chen Yi at 7:40 a.m. on 22 April, one of the first direct contacts between the two governments since the war.
Powell chased Zhou through the week and finally shook his hand at the Savoy Homann party; Payne recalled him challenging Zhou about American airmen held in China.
Payne first saw Powell holding a press conference at Manila airport and travelled on with him; her oral history is a main source for his conduct at Bandung.
When Payne's Sterno ran out, Wright helped her heat her hot comb with pure alcohol, an episode she still laughed about thirty years later.
Romulo was on Payne's flight from Manila to Indonesia with Powell.
On 1 April Dulles and the CIA's Wisner agreed that Powell's trip was unhelpful; Powell went anyway and came home to a warm Washington welcome.
On 5 May Malik gave Dulles a much bleaker reading of Bandung than the one Dulles had given the Cabinet a week earlier.
Barnett, a China specialist, failed to get an interview but watched Zhou at public events and at Nehru's house and built his account around Zhou's rise during the week.

threads_out.note: At Paris the Japanese proposal for a racial-equality clause was set aside and Nguyen Ai Quoc's petition for Vietnamese rights went unanswered. At Bandung equality of all races was one of the ten principles, and Pham Van Dong, Ho Chi Minh's comrade since the 1920s, led the Democratic Republic of Vietnam's delegation and called on Zhou on 21 April. Lebanon and Syria, mandates of the post-1919 settlement, came as sovereign states.

Kotelawala's question, whether the Soviet-controlled states of Eastern Europe were colonies, was an argument about the postwar order whose outlines were drawn at Yalta. The communiqué's formula, colonialism in all its manifestations, let the delegates disagree over it without naming it.

Adam Clayton Powell Jr. came to Bandung as Harlem's congressman and pastor of Abyssinian Baptist Church, the church his father had led through the Harlem Renaissance; Richard Wright had come to Harlem in 1937 as that generation faded. Wright's Color Curtain took up Du Bois's question of the colour line on a world scale.

Ten years after the surrender, Takasaki led Japan's first large delegation to an Asian gathering since the war and expressed regret for the damage Japan had done. Romulo, who had served on MacArthur's staff from Bataan to the return to Leyte, sat in the same hall.

Nehru and Pakistan's Mohammad Ali were co-sponsors at Bogor and opponents in Bandung: Nehru's note named Pakistan the most aggressive delegation, and the Kashmir dispute surfaced indirectly in the debates, eight years after partition.
